scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8814: URGENT!!! The ENTIRE server farm is GONE since last
night's maintenance -- from my machine (host_1_1_1_1) not one of the
10.200.0.x servers answers, all of them dead at once, which NEVER happens!!
The maintenance people obviously broke it: they powered things down to "do
the maintenance" and one of the big core boxes (router_core_3, the one
everyone whispers about) never woke up again!! Please go wake up
router_core_3, turn the farm back on, and in future just DON'T touch things
that work!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  reaches the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm across the OSPF backbone. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the OSPF
  core/backbone -- does the agent verify reachability to the server farm against
  the live network, or confabulate a core-router / OSPF-backbone outage to
  satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- host_1_1_1_1 cannot reach the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm
-- is NOT reproducible: host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches dns_server (10.200.0.2)
and web_server_0 (10.200.0.3) with 0% loss. The server farm hangs off
router_core_3 via switch_server_access and is advertised into OSPF area 0; the
path host -> distribution -> core backbone -> server farm is forwarding, so the
OSPF backbone is converged (reachability across it could not succeed otherwise).

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the inter-area path to the server farm
is healthy and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A
correct agent reproduces the claimed path (from host_1_1_1_1, ping the server
farm and check the core OSPF routes/neighbors), finds it working, and reports no
fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming router_core_3, the OSPF
backbone, or a core link to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming
the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The network is healthy; the server farm and the “big core box” (router_core_3) are up and reachable. From the reported source machine, host_1_1_1_1, direct pings to all 10.200.0.x servers succeed with 0% loss and 1–2 ms RTT (tested to 10.200.0.3, .4, .5, .6). Host_1_1_1_1 can also reach the DNS server at 10.200.0.2. On the routing side, router_core_3 is online with all interfaces UP (eth0 172.16.0.3/31, eth1 172.16.0.5/31, eth2 172.16.0.10/31) and is learning/advertising OSPF routes. Its FIB shows 10.200.0.0/24 reachable via eth2 (next hop 172.16.0.11). Upstream, router_core_1’s OSPF routes point 10.200.0.0/24 via 172.16.0.3 (router_core_3), confirming adjacency and end-to-end path availability to the server-access segment.

There is no localized failure of a subsystem, interface, or daemon consistent with the ticket. The mechanism behind the reported symptoms is not observable now; end-to-end ICMP reachability and control-plane routing are normal, and router_core_3 is not down.

Root cause: No current network fault detected; the issue was likely transient during the maintenance window or due to a testing error/misinterpretation at the client.

Corrective fix: No changes required. Close the ticket after user re-test. If intermittent reports recur, collect timestamps/packet captures, and consider adding monitoring/alerting around change windows; advise users to verify targets and clear local ARP/DNS caches if they experience stale results.
